title: Standardized Prostate Cancer Care
subtitle: Decision support inside the electronic health record

slides.title: Standardized Prostate Cancer Care
slides.standfirst: A decision support system integrated with the electronic health record, helping primary care physicians refer patients into Sweden's standardized care process for prostate cancer.

bullets.text: UX Lead
Ensure SCP referrals contain adequate information
More people receive prostate cancer care on time

slides.notes: State the objective in its clinical form immediately. This project's success criterion is not satisfaction or task time — it is referrals that do not come back.

slides.title: An incomplete referral is returned, queried or delayed
slides.standfirst: And the delay lands on the patient at exactly the point where time matters most.

bullets.text: Timely prostate cancer care depends on primary care physicians referring correctly and completely.
The referral decision happens inside a general consultation, under time pressure.
In a system built for general practice, not for one cancer pathway.

callout.text: Support a specialist decision inside a generalist workflow, without adding steps to a consultation that has none to spare — and do it within an existing EHR rather than as a separate tool.

slides.notes: Three constraints in one sentence: specialist content, generalist context, zero spare time. Say them separately, then together.

slides.title: What a standardized care process is
slides.standfirst: SCP defines the pathway a suspected cancer case should follow, with expected timings. Entry to it is the referral — which makes the referral the single highest-leverage document in the pathway.

bullets.text: The pathway is standardized. The entry point is not.
Every returned referral resets the clock for that patient.
Physicians are not resisting the process; they are working inside a record system that does not know about it.

slides.notes: Be careful not to blame primary care here. The framing that survived clinician review is that the record system is the thing that lacks the knowledge.

slides.title: A five-part workshop series, carrying the design forward in visible increments
slides.standfirst: Planning, Defining, Create concepts, Development — with clinicians in the room at every increment.
slides.notes: Visible increments is the phrase to use. Each workshop opened by showing what the last one produced, which is what kept participation high across a year.

slides.notes: Four steps is the whole interaction. If the audience is a clinical one, walk each; if not, summarise and move to the trade-off.

slides.title: Structure against flexibility
slides.standfirst: Guaranteeing that referrals contain adequate information pushes toward a rigid, mandatory-field form. Fitting into a live primary care consultation pushes toward the opposite.

bullets.text: The form is abandoned mid-consultation, or filled with placeholder values to get past it.
The referral is incomplete, and comes back — which is the original problem.
Rigid where the pathway genuinely requires a value; open everywhere else.

callout.text: Not only with clinicians, but with the EHR company, whose platform constraints shaped what was buildable at all.

slides.notes: This is the slide that generalises. Every clinical form in existence is somewhere on this dial, usually set by accident.

slides.title: Mutual understanding with the vendor became an explicit output
slides.standfirst: Working through the structure-versus-flexibility trade-off with the EHR company required each side learning the other's constraints — and the project treated that as a deliverable rather than a byproduct.

slides.title: Three things this project taught that outlived it

cards.title: Guidelines before concepts
cards.text: Agreeing explicit design guidelines in workshop one meant every later disagreement could be settled against a shared reference instead of by seniority.

cards.title: Observe both extremes
cards.text: A design validated only in the calm setting fails in the acute one. The emergency room field study changed what the interface could assume.

cards.title: The vendor is a stakeholder
cards.text: In embedded clinical software, platform constraints are design constraints. Discovering them late means redesigning; discovering them together means shipping.

slides.notes: The middle card is the one clinical audiences respond to. The third is the one product audiences respond to. Pick your emphasis.

slides.title: Specialist decisions have to be supported inside generalist workflows
slides.standfirst: The instinct is to build the cancer pathway a tool of its own. But primary care physicians do not live in one pathway; they live in a consultation, and every pathway that asks them to leave it loses.

callout.text: Not that the tool was used. That the referral did not come back — and that the patient's clock never restarted.

slides.notes: End on the clock. It reconnects a form-design problem to the reason anyone funded it.
